paras: The Montgomery County Klan intimidation was a campaign in the weeks before July 5, 1919, in which white residents of Montgomery County, Maryland, organized a "Ku Klux Klan" and white gangs terrorized Black men during a hunt for a Black man accused of assaulting women. The Baltimore Afro-American reported that the group also meant to keep the area's Black population "in order"; no deaths or injuries were reported.

According to a Washington dispatch dated July 5, an unidentified "colored maniac" was accused of assaulting a Black teacher, Miss M. Simmons, and then several white women, the latest Mary Saunders. The story gives the number of white women as both five and four.

White citizens formed searching parties across the county and near the District of Columbia line, more than twenty people were arrested and released when the victim failed to identify them, and nearly $2,500 in rewards was offered. Meanwhile, the paper said, white gangs terrorized several "innocent colored men," whom it did not name. Besides finding the criminal, the Klan intended "to keep the colored people of the entire section in order." A partly lost passage tied this to labor, saying whites were dissatisfied that work was done only "under the best conditions and at their own prices" and that the "Klan" would act "by inspiring fear and violence if necessary."

Bishop I. N. Ross of the A.M.E. Church said the District's colored citizens would help capture the assailant but asked "that there be no mob violence" and that the law administer punishment. No report of the assailant's capture or of action against the Klan appears in the coverage.

The Afro-American ran the story on its July 11 front page under the headline "Keep Negroes in Order," continuing it on page 4. It called the accused man a "maniac" and "madman" but set "Klan" in quotation marks, stressed the innocence of the men targeted, and printed the bishop's appeal against mob violence. In its telling, the Klan's purpose reached beyond one manhunt to control of Black residents and their labor.

accounts.label: Black correspondent (special from Washington)
accounts.gist: Assaults on women by an unidentified Black man led white citizens to form a 'Ku Klux Klan' and searching parties; white gangs terrorized innocent Black men, and the Klan meant also to keep Black residents 'in order' and to use fear and violence over labor terms.

accounts.label: Bishop I. N. Ross
accounts.gist: Black citizens of the District shared the anger over the alleged assaults and would help find the criminal, but asked for no mob violence.

framing.detail: The Baltimore Afro-American headlined the story 'Keep Negroes in Order', called the men terrorized 'innocent', put 'Klan' in quotation marks, and printed Bishop Ross's appeal against mob violence, while calling the accused assailant a 'colored maniac' and 'madman'.

four ('four white women in succession', with Mary Saunders 'the fifth victim' overall; deck reads 'One Colored and Four')

conflicts.note: Internal inconsistency within the same story; the body and deck agree on four white women and five victims in all.
